script: Ninety days of bookkeeping. That is all a Lagos market trader needs before Ledgerfold can offer a working-capital loan. Adaeze Nwachukwu founded Ledgerfold after years in microfinance, where she saw traders turn their stock every few weeks with no credit to match. Traders keep their books free in the app, borrow for fourteen to sixty days, and repay from daily sales. In March 2026, the company reported 6,400 active traders and a loan book of $410,000. Ledgerfold is raising $2.5 million in a priced seed round. I'm an AI presenter, summarising the company's own figures.

This is an AI-presented summary of Tarmacly's pitch. On the Kano to Lagos corridor, most trucks are still booked by phone, and carriers wait weeks to be paid. Musa Garba-Lawal built Tarmacly to fix both. Shippers post loads. Tarmacly matches them with vetted truck owners, tracks every trip, and pays carriers within forty-eight hours through a partner bank. The company reports 180 contracted shippers, 2,300 trucks, and about $1.1 million in monthly freight value in early 2026. The ask is an $8 million Series A, to open the Abuja to Onitsha corridor.

In Benue State, a yam harvest can lose much of its value before it reaches a buyer. Yamfield Agro, founded by Terna Iorliam, puts solar cold rooms at rural markets. Farmers pay per crate, per day, with mobile money. Yamfield also buys part of the stored produce at an agreed floor price. It is early. Two pilot rooms have run since August 2025, and 310 farmers have used them. Yamfield is raising $400,000 on a SAFE, to build eight more rooms and prove the economics site by site. I'm an AI presenter, and these are the company's reported figures.

I'm an AI presenter, sharing the pitch for Clinicrest, from Ibadan. Its founder, Dr. Folake Adebayo-Hart, watched clinics run out of essential medicines every month. Clinicrest pairs an inventory app that forecasts each clinic's needs with next-day delivery from its own licensed warehouse. One point deserves care. The deck counts 340 active clinics and pharmacies. The latest management accounts list 212 paying accounts. The company says the difference is free trials, but has not yet shown the split. Clinicrest is raising $1.8 million in a priced seed round, for two new depots.

Diesel is one of the largest costs a Nigerian market trader carries. Marketlight Grids, led by Hauwa Bello-Idris in Abuja, replaces it. Each market cluster gets a solar and battery mini-grid, and every shop gets a prepaid smart meter. Traders top up with mobile money. Marketlight owns and maintains the grid, under a fifteen-year concession. Fourteen grids are live, serving 4,100 shops, with a reported collection rate of ninety-six percent. Marketlight is raising $12 million in equity, for thirty more grids. This summary is presented by an AI presenter.

An AI presenter here, with Tallyloom's pitch. Payroll in Nigeria and Ghana means tax, pension and statutory filings, every single month. Babajide Coker's company, Tallyloom, computes and files them, pays staff through bank integrations, and keeps an audit trail ready for inspection. It serves 1,250 employers and 186,000 employee seats. Annual recurring revenue was $6.4 million at December 2025, according to its audited accounts. Tallyloom is raising a $22 million Series B, to enter Kenya and add salary advances with a bank partner.

Ajo, the rotating savings circle, is how millions of Nigerians save. It runs on trust, and on WhatsApp. Temitope Alade's Ajopot runs it on rails instead. Contributions are debited on schedule, the payout order is fixed up front, and the money is held by a licensed partner bank. In March 2026, Ajopot reported 18,700 active users across 3,900 circles. Revenue is still small, a one percent payout fee, and the company says so. It is raising 1.2 billion naira on a SAFE. I'm an AI presenter, sharing Ajopot's pitch.

I'm an AI presenter, and this is Maji Loop. In Nairobi's informal settlements, families often pay more per litre for water than wealthier neighbourhoods do. Wanjiru Kamau founded Maji Loop to run solar-pumped kiosks that filter and dispense clean water by the litre, paid with M-Pesa or a tag. Revenue is shared with the utility under a service contract. The company reports ninety-six kiosks, about 38,000 households served each month, and 41 million litres sold in 2025. Maji Loop is raising $1.5 million in a priced seed round, for 150 more kiosks.

A fish trader at a Ghanaian landing beach has hours, not days, before the catch spoils. Kwabena Asante-Mensah started Nsuo Labs in Tema to buy back those hours, with a solar ice plant on the beach and insulated crates rented by the day. One pilot site has run since November 2025, with 140 regular traders. In a small survey, traders reported spoilage falling from about a quarter of the catch to under a tenth. That is self-reported, and early. Nsuo Labs is raising $600,000 on a SAFE. I'm an AI presenter, sharing the company's pitch.

An AI presenter, sharing Brightkloof Energy's pitch. Thandiwe Mokoena's company gives South African small businesses rooftop solar and batteries, with no upfront cost. Brightkloof designs, installs, monitors and maintains each system, for a fixed monthly fee over ten years. It reports 2,900 contracted sites and 38 megawatts installed. The company is also clear that growth slowed as load-shedding eased in 2025. Brightkloof is raising 280 million rand in Series B equity, to expand into KwaZulu-Natal and the Western Cape.

Cairo has thousands of neighbourhood kiosks, and most of them order stock by phone, from many distributors, with little access to credit. Souqsheet, led by Mariam El-Sayed, brings that ordering into one Android app, with simple stock tracking and seven-day supplier credit from a partner bank. The company reports 9,800 kiosks ordering each month, and about $4.2 million in monthly order value. It is raising a $6 million Series A, to reach Upper Egypt. I'm an AI presenter, and this is Souqsheet's pitch.

I'm an AI presenter, here with Kazikit's pitch. In Kenya, informal building contractors, the fundis, quote from memory and chase payment by phone. Brian Mwangi built Kazikit for them: a light Android app for quoting with local material prices, tracking spend per job, and sending M-Pesa payment requests. Since September 2025, 1,900 contractors have signed up, and around 600 use it weekly. There is no revenue yet. Kazikit is raising $350,000 on a SAFE, to launch a paid tier and a materials marketplace.
